sections.text: Introduction

There are many established ASTM tests of practical 
 significance that can be applied to insulating oil. Some of these tests are 
 more applicable to new oils than to service-aged oils; some are more useful in 
 the analysis of service-aged oils than oils received in new condition.

Each of the tests and their 
 significance are described. While the number following the name of the test is 
 the number of the ASTM Standard Method.

sections.text:
Electrical Tests
 Dielectric Breakdown Voltage

The dielectric breakdown voltage of insulating oil is a measure of its ability 
to withstand voltage stress without failure. It is the voltage at which 
breakdown occurs between two electrodes under prescribed test conditions. The 
test serves primarily to indicate the presence of electrically conductive 
contaminants in the oil, such as dissolved water, dirt, or particulate matter.

A high dielectric breakdown voltage does not indicate the absence of all 
contaminants, however.

Three methods are recognized for measuring the 
dielectric breakdown voltage of insulating oils:

ASTM D1816-79 (24) is the preferred method for 
testing fluid that is being proceed into apparatus or contained in new 
apparatus. As the method is more 
sensitive to very small amounts of contaminants, it should not be used for, 
acceptance testing of new, unprocessed fluids as received from a vendor. Its 
significance for evaluating service-aged oils is being determined. This method 
uses spherically shaped electrodes. The gap distance can be varied, but standard 
settings are 0.04 in and 0.08 in.

ASTM D877-79 (23) 
 is recommended for the routine 
acceptance of new, unprocessed oil from a vendor. This test method uses 
flat-faced cylindrical electrodes with a 0.01in gap.

IEC 156-63 (10) method applies 
to either acceptance 
tests on new deliveries of insulating liquids, or testing of treated 
liquids prior to or during filling into electrical equipment, or to monitoring and maintenance of 
oil-filled apparatus in service. This 
method uses spherical or partially spherical of shape electrodes with a 2.5 in 
gap.

sections.text:
Power Factor/
Dissipation Factor

The dissipation factor 
is a measure of the power lost when an electrical insulating liquid is subjected 
to an arc field. The power is dissipated as heat within the fluid.

A low-value dissipation 
factor means that the fluid will cause little of the applied power to be lost.

The test is used as a 
check on the deterioration and contamination of insulating oil because of its 
sensitivity to ionic contaminants.
Resistivity

The resistivity of a liquid is a measure of its 
electrical insulating properties under conditions comparable to those of the 
test. High resistivity reflects low content of free ions and ion-forming 
particles, and normally indicates a low concentration of conductive 
contaminants.
Chemical Tests
Copper Corrosion

This test is designed to 
detect the presence of free sulfur and combined corrosive sulfur by how the 
liquid affects polished copper strips in prescribed conditions.

The test indicates the 
possibility of corrosion inside of electrical equipment resulting from the 
presence of sulfur-containing compounds. The source of sulfur present in 
insulating oil is usually the crude oil from which it is refined.
Acid Number

The acid number of an electrical insulating liquid is a measure
of the acidic components of that material. In new oil, any acid present is
likely residual from the refining process.

In a service-aged liquid, the
neutralization number is a measure of acidic byproducts of the oxidation of an
oil.

The acid number may be used as a general guide for determination
of when oil should be reprocessed or replaced. IP 1/64 is the
traditional color-change indicator method of titrating the acids with the mild
(0.1 N) KOH solution.

Water in Insulating Liquids: 
(Karl Fisher Method)

Water may be present in insulating liquids in several forms. The
presence of free water may be indicated by visual examination. The oil will
appear cloudy or separated water drops will be seen, probably on the bottom
surface.

The presence of free water can be 
remedied by filtration or other means. Dissolved water cannot be detected 
visually and is normally measured by physical or chemical means. Dissolved water 
affects the dielectric breakdown of oil and is more commonly present in oil than 
free water.

The method cited is suitable for 
determination of dissolved water in insulating oil, which depending upon 
conditions of sample handling and methods of analysis.

The units of measure of water are 
parts per million (ppm). New insulating oil received from the manufacture 
normally contains less than 35 (ppm) it should be tested for moisture content to 
avoid introducing high moisture-content oil into electrical equipment.
